summary: Describes a general-purpose SSH authentication method for interactive logins, where the user types data on a keyboard or similar device. Its main goal is to let the client support many kinds of authentication mechanisms without knowing the details of each one.

eli5.summary: The server asks questions and shows them on screen, and you type the answers. The client simply passes along whatever is asked, without knowing the secret rules behind it.

subtitle: One SSH login method where the server sends the prompts and the client just shows them and passes back the answers.

tldr.problem: Existing SSH authentication methods are tightly tied to specific mechanisms, so adding a new one means updating every client.
tldr.mechanism: The keyboard-interactive method lets the server send prompts as text, and the client displays them, collects typed answers and returns them, without knowing what mechanism sits behind them.
tldr.outcome: Servers can add or change mechanisms such as challenge-response or one-time passwords without client changes, but only for mechanisms that need no special client code.

today: RFC 4256 is a Proposed Standard from January 2006, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Generic Method
sections.content:
The SSH authentication protocol (RFC 4252) is a general-purpose user authentication protocol that runs over the SSH transport layer (RFC 4253). Methods defined so far are tightly coupled to the mechanism underneath. Adding a new mechanism means every client must be updated.

This RFC defines the keyboard-interactive method. The client needs little or no knowledge of the mechanism the server uses, because all authentication data is entered on the keyboard. The server can then select or change mechanisms without client updates. If a separate authentication layer such as PAM is used, the server may not need code changes either.

Challenge-response and one-time password mechanisms are easily supported. The limit is that the method works only for mechanisms that need no special client code, such as hardware drivers or password mangling.
sections.eli5: Imagine a doorman who just reads out whatever question the building asks and writes down your answers. The doorman never needs to learn new rules when the building changes its questions.

sections.title: The Initial Request
sections.content:
The client starts with an SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST carrying the user name, the service name, the method name keyboard-interactive, a language tag and a submethods field.

The language tag is deprecated and SHOULD be the empty string. The server SHOULD choose the language from the tags exchanged during key exchange instead. The submethods field is a comma-separated list of preferred submethods. The client MAY fill it if it knows the user's preference, otherwise it MUST send the empty string. How the server interprets it is implementation-dependent.

No password is sent in this first message, unlike the password method. The server MUST answer with success, failure or an information request. It SHOULD NOT send a failure just because the user name or service name is wrong. Instead it SHOULD send requests that look like the normal ones and fail later, after a suitable delay, so that valid user names cannot be found by comparing results.
sections.eli5: The client says who it is and that it can answer questions typed on a keyboard. It does not send a secret yet. The server should act the same whether or not the name is real, so nobody can guess names.

sections.title: Requests and Responses
sections.content:
The server sends SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_REQUEST with a name, an instruction, a language tag, a number of prompts, and for each prompt a text and an echo flag. The server may send as many requests as needed, but MUST NOT have more than one outstanding. The name and instruction fields MAY be empty; the prompts MUST NOT be. The number of prompts may be 0.

The client replies with SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_RESPONSE, holding a count and the answers in prompt order. Responses are UTF-8, so a client that reads input in another encoding MUST convert. If the counts do not match, the server MUST send a failure. If there were zero prompts, the client MUST send a response with zero answers.

If authentication fails, the server SHOULD send a failure rather than ask again. It should send multiple requests only when it needs additional data, for example because several mechanisms must all succeed. Before a failure it MAY delay; a suggested default is 2 seconds. Systems that handle non-ASCII passwords SHOULD normalize them, using SASLprep where they both store and compare passwords.
sections.eli5: The server asks, the client answers in the same order, and the server asks again only if it truly needs more. If the answers are wrong, the server says no and waits a moment first.

sections.title: How Clients Show Prompts
sections.content:
The RFC includes user interface guidance because some protocol details exist for UI reasons. A command-line client SHOULD print the name and instruction, if non-empty, then show each prompt and read the input. A graphical client might use the name as a dialog title and the prompts as labels for entry fields, with all prompts in one dialog.

Clients MUST handle instructions with embedded newlines, SHOULD be able to show at least 30 characters of name and prompt, and MAY truncate longer ones as long as there is an obvious sign of truncation. They SHOULD NOT truncate the instruction. They SHOULD filter control characters to avoid terminal-control attacks.

The echo flag says whether typed characters should be shown. A client that does not honor it MUST err on the side of masking. Clients SHOULD NOT add characters like a colon to the prompt, and MUST accept and pass on empty answers.
sections.eli5: The client should show what the server says without changing it, hide what you type when told to, and make it clear if it had to shorten a long message.

sections.title: Worked Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples. The first is a challenge-response login with a handheld token: the server sends the instruction The challenge is '14315716' with one prompt, the user types the token's answer, and the server replies with success. The RFC notes this is not possible with the other authentication methods.

The second is a password login where the password has expired. After the first password the server sends a second request with two prompts to enter and repeat a new password, then a request with zero prompts that tells the user the password was changed. The client answers that with a zero-answer response, and the server ends with success.
sections.eli5: In the first example, the server shows a puzzle number, you read the answer from a little gadget, and you are in. In the second, the server says your password is old, asks for a new one twice, and then lets you in.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The method depends on the security of the underlying SSH transport layer. Without its confidentiality, any authentication data could be intercepted.

The number of exchanges can vary, and the RFC warns that an observer who counts them may learn something. For example, an observer might guess that a password has expired and, with more observation, work out the password lifetime a site imposes.

For IANA, the userauth type is keyboard-interactive, and the method-specific message constants are SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_REQUEST (60) and SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_RESPONSE (61).
sections.eli5: The conversation is only private because the SSH tunnel around it is private. Even so, someone watching could notice how many questions were asked and guess something from that.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_REQUEST
messages.note: Name, instruction and prompts with echo flags.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_RESPONSE
messages.note: One answer per prompt, in order.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS
messages.note: Or a failure, or another info request.
